I loved Uplink, and tried all the games that it spawned (Hacker: Evolution etc) only to be disappointed.  Finally, with Hacknet, a true successor has come along and hit all the right spots to make me love it.  Being nosey not only rewards you with nice little humorous skits, but can actually give you links to different servers with rewards of their own.  Breaking different ports with different software and laughing at silly bosses insisting on crap passwords could even raise awareness of security issues in real life.  The length isn't massive, but nor is the price so it is worth it.

On top of all the mechanics and semi-realistic approach... it is great fun!  It will clearly only appeal to people who are interested in hacking games, but if you (like me) wanted more Uplink, then this is the game you have been waiting for.  Highly recommended.
Addictive

TL:DR I'm very pleased with the money spent, would recommend and even bought some copies for friends. (Looking forward to MP one day)

Release bugs aside (Only read about, never experienced) the game was very enjoyable. Does a good job of making you feel  like a "1337 h4x0r" while having a decent narrative that is delivered in a very organic way. Not a huge game, even completing all the side stuff can be done in under 10 hours, but I would say it was a very memorable experience. There are plenty of references to internet culture, neat little easter eggs tucked away if you use all the tools available to you.

A worthy successor to Uplink and other such hacker titles of the past, with a fresh new coat of paint. Being able to operate menus by mouse or through terminal commands is nice. Without giving too much away it is actually important to know the basic navigation commands rather than always using the mouse though. But having the option is great, especially when time is of the essence. 

The puzzles are fairly straight forward, but still engaging, with information scattered about on different systems, files, hidden and encrypted. Just a tip to new players, IRC logs are purely fluff that are randomly generated  along with several other elements of the game (to keep each playthrough fresh). you will not find mission relevant data in an IRC chat log.

It's everything your little dorito-stained heart could desire.

[h1]General[/h1]
Tthis "small" game has a lot of features to be honest. Either way, if you love to work with command line interface's (CLI) or you like to mess around with it, go ahead and get this kind of game. It's indeed a hacking simulator however, I don't think it's that realstic. Systems have more security in real life than in the game ofcourse. Don't expect to be a hacker after playing this game :')

[h1]Features[/h1]
Anyway, yes - the game has a nice structure and every detail is gorgeous. It has a kind of a storyline but via contracts. You work for peope/companies and do small tasks. With easy tools that are located on your pc (in the game) you can use them as a command and mess around with it - with that I mean ... exploit ports, overload proxyservers, send internet worms, crack SSH port and more!  It's all about digging around, and because of this you might find hilarious IRC quote's and other data that you need  - even scripts. But sometimes it's not easy as you can get tracked down when you start to hack someone's system.. or another hacker removes one of your system files so you can't use your GUI anymore, then you are forced to use your CLI. 

The game is also newbie-friendly, just type "help" and you can see all the commands that you need while playing the game. It won't get bored ... not at all - I love this kind of stuff so I can't dislike it, not at all.

There's so much to say ... just try it out c:

I [b]recommend[/b] this game for all people. Really, it's fun and the ending - when you finish last quest of Bit - is amazing.

Incredibly fun game, I have nothing but praise. Great inclusion of some unix based command line utilities. reminds me of the epxloits available in archlinux... this game definitly has that "black hat feel". there is no understatement in the creators quote *im paraphrasing* "looks so real you would dare play it in an airport". When I started playing, I was blown away by the way this game seamlessly brings the thrill of penitration testing with the simplicity you would hope could hold ANYONE's interest... It isnt so in depth that it is frustrating but it is just emmersive enough to spike real curiosity. I think this game may inspire a small portion of its players to look at whats really out there maybe delve into the world of cybersecurity. if your a programmer or linux person, THIS GAME IS FOR YOU! but if your just curious, THIS GAME IS ALSO FOR YOU! I also love that this game can be played with good or malicious intentions. it would be nice to see a way to edit the UI manually maybe give players a chance to make their own "x-server" layouts. also what about expanding the shell to run remote commands, not just trap and overload.
It's like the spiritual successor to Uplink, and I loved Uplink!

This game's trailer does NOT do it justice. It's great that it looks good, but it's also really clever too! Well worth my money. If you've always wanted to try a hack sim, but weren't sure if it would live up to your expectations, I can assure you that this one will.

Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

reviews.review:
Hacknet is a hacking simulation in the vein of Introversion's fantastic Uplink. It provides the player a virtual OS from which to interact with 'nodes' dotted around the map. Each node represents a computer system which can be approached using the software and hardware knowledge you accumulate throughout the game. Pretty simple stuff on the surface, but Hacknet is a fantastically well-designed story-driven experience, with considerable replay value which will only continue to grow as new content is invariably released.

This game deserves praise for it's graphics, in that they perfectly fit the tone of the game. In most other game genres we typically see a push toward more cutting-edge photo-realism, but here we have a clean, crisp environment that doesn't over-burden or confuse the player with menus and tedious repetitive interaction. Praise is also due to the sound design in this title. The music is, again, a perfect fit for the game's tone. Orchesteral strings move to thumping bass adding a sense of pressure and drive that has kept me going back just for the music.


There are some problems with this game however. Some people will say these aren't problems as such, more personal gripes, but take them however you wish. 

1. It's short. Like really short. With no experience whatsoever, my first run was just under 3 hours from start to finish, completing every avaliable mission in the game aside from 'Junebug' which was bugged at the time. Hopefully, more content will be added soon, and the ability to open story creation to the community is an exciting prospect shound it be considered.

2. It's easy. The learning curve is pretty shallow, with a few basic commands covering every action you will be performing. Once you have got launching cracks using the TAB key down to a fine art, you can smash through any security in next to no time.

3. No Upgrade abilities. A key component of every computer interface is the hardware it's connected to, and in a game setting the ability to upgrade and customise that hardware is a given. There is no such system here. The only resource you have is RAM, which is set throughout the game and cannot be improved upon. This does give the game a streamlined feel, but I would still rather have an functioning economy and avenues to explore with my earnings.

Overall, I think Hacknet deserves your time if you enjoy the genre. If you do enjoy this quite esoteric game style, then you've no doubt played the alternatives. On balance, I would say that Onlink, the fan-made re-write of Uplink is the superior game in this category still. It is a longer, more challenging experience. That being said, with expansion and dedication, Hacknet will become the standard by which all other hacking simulation games will be judged. We should all help it get there, and enjoy the rewards when they come.

Buy it.

The spiritual successor to Uplink you've been waiting for.

This is a game that makes you feel like a real hacker. You type in a terminal to perform most functions, but don't let that alienate you, because you do it with only a dozen or so commands that are easy to remember. You'll pick it up as you go. But where it really shines is that it captures the same spirit of exploration and "Can I really do this...? YES I CAN!!" that made Uplink fantastic. There are some moments where the puzzles give you JUST enough information that you have to think - not by game logic, but real logic, about what to do - and it feels amazing when it pays off. It's not without flaws, being a new release at the time of writing, but save for one or two wallbanging moments it plays very smoothly. If you've played Uplink and want more (or felt that there was too much time/money management in that and would try a similar game with more story) Hacknet is for you. If you haven't played Uplink, play it first, because it has some shining moments but will feel extremely dated after the modern polish of Hacknet.

I was hoping this would be a little more like Uplink, however 2 hours in and I seem to be stuck in a very linear story line. Which is fine if you like that sort of thing, I was hoping for more of an Uplink/sandbox hacking simulator. Pick your own missions, complete them how you wish, buy upgrades for your gateway and rig, etc.

Make no mistake: Hacknet is the best hacker simulator this side of Uplink. It's fun to play and its missions require a decent amount of thought without ever really being overly "gotchya". What absolutely destroys the game is the sheer number of game-ending bugs and fail-states. Over the course of my dozen or so hours with the game, I've run into the different bugs that have caused me to have to start the game over because I can't progress. These fail-states are slowly but surely getting patched, but until they are all taken care of I can't possibly recommend this game.

Pretty cool game. Not very long. I had it beat in about 5 hours, but for what it was, it was pretty fun to play. Playing it again years later (including the DLC this time), I'm doing a 180 and state that this is a pretty amazing game in its own right and shouldn't be compared to uplink et all.

Yeah there's no upgrading your rig and the memory indicator is just for show, but you do upgrade your capabilities with new skills (port hacks and some utilities) and my earlier description of simple hacking animations and all was not fair. The required hacks vary both in combination and in speed and really presents you with a challange at times to time it right or do it in the right order to maximize your memory usage.

Aside from that there are lots of 'find clue's' quests, try to scan around and expand your pathways. There are tons of interesting content to read and the whole game feels like an homage to the security community as well as like minded games of old (including Uplink). The whole thing is a love letter.

So best story so far while playing this game:

Doing my first aggressive hack, start by shelling the proxy and immediately get a ping warning.
Start hacking the ports like a boss, get into the system with 20 seconds to spare.
Barge into the logs and rm everything, then find the file I need and rm that as well.
Look down and panic as the countdown is at 3.
Logs finish. 2
File deletes. 1
Screen blacks, system reboot initiates.
After my system reboots, I get warning saying my firewall has been circumvented.
Panic again and forkbomb my system.
Reboot to black screen, no GUI or anything.

Here's where the instruction segment comes in. After floundering around for a while I figured out what I needed to do:
-Scanned my own system to get the IP for FaceSpace Tech
-Connected to FaceSpace Tech
-Made my way down to the sys folder
-Copied over the x-server.sys
-Rebooted again

Now everything is cliche-hacker-green xD Need to regain my taskbar though, but until then this game gets a 10/10!

If you work with Linux at all, you'll probably find yourself pleasantly surprised by the functionality this game tries to replicate. There's also all sorts of interesting easter eggs and other content to find, even after you've beaten the game once.

One of my favorite games now, definitely. I highly recommend this if you like puzzle games, or even if this sort of theme is appealing to you - the game pulls it off really well with the UI, visuals, sound, and even the writing and the story.

[h1]TL;DR[/h1]
A great hacking game with a story too linear. 8/10

People are saying Hacknet is Uplink but better. I'm saying Hacknet is a derivative work of Uplink.

Uplink can be seen as an "open world" game. The goal is simple; do contract work, get money, upgrade your stuff. There's a "story" involved but you can completely ignore it if you so wish.

Hacknet is more linear. There isn't much beside the story. There is contract work, but its point is to just advance in the story. You're locked out of some of the contract work after advancing through a certain point in the story. You cannot get money or upgrade your gear, you're limited to the same amount of RAM and power you have.

Based on what I said, Hacknet can be seen as a bad game, but it's everything but bad. The gameplay is amazing. The interface is well fit for what it's used for. The story is very appealing and really clutches on you to take you with it.

The game simulates a command line environment quite well, but is missing some really basic stuff you'd expect to find. The tab autocomplete is lacking. You cannot create files or folders, so you're locked to any files or folders the game gives you. There isn't a text editor, so your only way of editing files to use a [i]replace[/i] command. Then again, the game clearly isn't directed at experienced command line users, but rather to newcomers (or "skiddies", the game even calls you such at one point) who may have never used a command line.

Doing the hacking is not complicated at all. You don't have to memorise complicated command calls or signatures, you just run the right command at the right time. Most of the time you don't even need to use the command line, since usually there's a button to click or a scrollbar to drag.

I was expecting a tad more realistic simulation of a command line, but the game is really good nevertheless. It took me about 5 hours to beat, after of which there isn't anything sensible to do. There are small secrets scattered around to look for and discover, if you like easter egg hunting.
